content: Virola sebifera, commonly referred to as Ucuúba-do-Cerrado or red ucuúba, is a tree species belonging to the Myristicaceae family. It is native to regions of Central and South America. Virola sebifera is characterized as a tall and slender tree, capable of reaching heights of up to 30 meters. Its leaves are simple in structure and can grow up to 30 centimeters in length. The tree produces small, unisexual flowers that are arranged in panicles. Its fruit is reddish in color and oval in shape. Differentiating individual Virola species, which number between 40 and 60, can be challenging due to their similarities. The bark of Virola sebifera contains a high concentration of tannins and psychoactive compounds, including dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and 5-MeO-DMT. Indigenous communities utilize the bark for treating various skin conditions. The ripe seeds of the tree are rich in fatty acid glycerides, particularly laurodimyristin and trimyristin. The seeds of Virola sebifera are processed to extract yellow, aromatic fats that emit a scent reminiscent of nutmeg. However, these fats are prone to becoming rancid quickly. Industrially, these fats are used in the production of candles, soaps, and other fat-based products. The properties of Virola fat are comparable to those of cocoa butter or shea butter. In homeopathy, a product known as Myristica sebifera (abbreviated as Myris) is derived from the fresh, red juice extracted from the injured bark of the tree. This homeopathic remedy is commonly employed to treat conditions such as abscesses, phlegmon, paronychia, furuncles, anal fissures, infections of the parotid gland, and bacterial tonsillitis, among others. In traditional medicine, the smoke produced from the inner bark of the tree is used by shamans among indigenous Venezuelan communities to treat fever-related conditions. Additionally, the bark is sometimes cooked and used in rituals to expel malevolent spirits.
